steps: Plan the installation
Masonry wood-burning fireplace only: never factory-built, never a mobile home. Check the AHJ for permits and leave the door off until finishing work is done.

• Designed for a masonry wood-burning fireplace. Never install it in a factory-built fireplace or a mobile home.
  • Check with the authority having jurisdiction about restrictions, requirements and permits.
  • Confirm chimney height, ceiling clearance and hearth extension (Tables 1-3) before starting.
  • Use only certified components; never a temporary or makeshift installation.
  • Leave the door off until finishing work around the fireplace is done, to avoid scratches or damage.
RSF strongly recommends installers certified by the National Fireplace Institute (U.S.) or Wood Energy Technology Transfer Inc. (Canada).
Prepare the masonry fireplace

Fix the damper open or remove it; if the throat damper is removed or the masonry modified, mount metal plate #931022 (owner's manual bag) where it's visible inside the masonry hearth. Protect the hearth; two people to move the unit.
Check the chimney
Fireplace and chimney sound and built to NFPA 211 / CAN/CSA-B365, with no flue shared with another appliance. Don't remove bricks or mortar.

The masonry fireplace and chimney must be in good working condition and built to NFPA 211 (latest edition) or the applicable national, provincial, state or local codes. The installation conforms to CAN/CSA-B365.

Don't connect to a chimney flue serving another appliance. Don't remove bricks or mortar from the fireplace. Exception: masonry or steel, including the damper plate, may come off the smoke shelf and adjacent damper frame to fit a liner, as long as the structure isn't weakened and protection for combustibles stays at National Building Code levels.
Install the liner
Full-height 6" (152 mm) liner, or 5.5" (140 mm) with the taller minimum chimney, installed per the liner maker. Stove adapter on the bottom of a flexible liner; seal the damper area around the liner.
Set the insert & flue collar

Connect the liner straight to the factory-installed collar if there's room; otherwise move the collar onto the stove adapter, slide the insert in and bolt the collar back from inside. Level on the two front leveling bolts.

The appliance flue collar is provided and already installed.

  1. Room to connect directly: slide the insert into the fireplace opening, then connect and secure the liner to the flue collar.
  2. No room: remove the collar before the insert goes in. Take out the first three secondary air tubes from the left side (5/16" socket) and the baffle to reach the collar bolts, then remove the 4 collar bolts.
  3. Connect the stove adapter to the collar. Once it is secured, attach the pull-handle to the collar.
  4. Slide the insert in, centering the collar (now on the liner) over the opening in the top of the insert.
  5. With the unit on a flat surface, adjust the two front leveling bolts for stability.
  6. Reach up through the insert and pull the collar down until it contacts the top of the insert. Bolt it from inside the firebox with the four bolts provided.
  7. Remove the detachable pull-handle.
Refitting the baffle and secondary air tube (holes slightly upward, locking pin in) is described under Chimney cleaning.
Fit the trim
Five small bolts, 1/8 hex (Allen) key with the door open. Oblong holes give up to 1" of depth; use the recessed position for a shallower fireplace.
Install the refractory bricks
Before the first fire: rear brick (1), right and left sides (2, 3), soft insulation on the floor (4), bottom brick (5), then the two front bricks (6, 7).
Fit the ash lip
Angle the removable ash lip and lower it into place, with its rear edge behind the firebox's vertical lip.
Check mantel clearances
Combustible shelves at the Table 4 height for their depth (24" above the glass up to 8" deep); combustible posts up to 4" deep at least 9" from the glass.

panels.title: Smoke spills when the door opens
items: Door opened too fast → open slowly; let the pressure stabilize first
Blower running → switch it off before opening the door
Range hood / bath exhaust running → negative pressure; crack a window near the insert
Dirty chimney or plugged cap → clean it; screened caps clog with creosote
Liner below 6" with marginal chimney height → keep the 6" liner
Too little kindling → smoke during lighting

panels.title: Burns too fast / won't slow down
items: Leaking door seal or gasket → paper test, adjust latch pin / hinge, replace gasket
Hole in a secondary air tube → unwanted extra air
Air control has no effect → air leak; stop use until it's found
Excessive draft → hotter fire, shorter burns, less heat recovery

panels.title: Smolders or hard to light
items: Air closed too far or too fast → reopen, then close gradually
Door shut too soon at start-up → crack it another minute or two
Wet or unseasoned wood → excess visible smoke, poor burn
Weak draft → smoke in the room, hard to light (often mistaken for a blocked air intake)

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Build a top-down fire: small wood on the bottom, kindling and paper on top. It starts faster and burns cleaner.

  1. Move the combustion air control lever all the way open (to the right). You want as much air as possible.
  2. Behind the front bricks, lay 2-3 criss-crossed layers of small wood: about 10 pieces, 1" to 2" in diameter.
  3. Criss-cross about 20 pieces of finger-size kindling on top, then add a few pieces of paper.
  4. Light the top of the pile. Close the door most of the way, but not all the way. You should see air rushing in.
  5. After about 2 minutes, close the door completely. If the fire starts to smolder, crack the door for another minute or two. A tall chimney or cold weather means a little longer.
  6. When the startup fuel is mostly a bed of coals, rake the coals to the front and add cordwood, up to 6 logs. Lay the bottom layer front to back and the next layer left to right. Always use at least 2 criss-crossed layers.
  7. Keep the door cracked for a couple of minutes while the logs catch, then close it. Leave the air control wide open until your next reload.
Never use flammable liquids to start or freshen a fire. Never leave the fire burning with the door open or ajar; it can overfire and damage the insert. Don't use a grate or raise the fire.

air.title: The combustion air control
air.html:
This insert has no flue damper. The closed door seals the firebox, and the combustion air control lever sets how much air the fire gets.

Lever all the way rightFully open, most air
Moving it leftLess air into the firebox

Turning the fire down

  • Close the lever gradually, never from maximum to minimum in one move.
  • Watch how the fire reacts. If it starts to smolder or go out, open the air again and wait longer before you try.
  • If nothing changes, you can keep closing. In time you should be able to close the air all or most of the way.
  • Always keep visible flame. It keeps the glass and chimney liner clean.

Burning too fast? Turn the air down. Smoldering with no flames? Turn it up. Some installations can't hold a fire with the air fully closed, and that's normal.

The lever gets hot enough to burn. Use the handle or gloves provided. If moving it has no effect on the burn rate, air is leaking in, likely at the door. Stop using the insert until the leak is found and fixed.

reload.title: Reloading the fire
reload.html:
1. Have your next load ready before you open the door. The shorter the door is open, the hotter the firebox stays.
  2. If you have the optional blower, turn it off. A running fan can push smoke out of the insert.
  3. Open the door slowly so smoke doesn't spill into the room.
  4. Poke and stir the unburned wood to revive the fire, then add the new logs.
  5. Keep a clear path in front of the "pilot": the metal tube centered between the two andiron posts. It brings air close to the coals.
  6. Leave the door slightly ajar for a couple of minutes until the new wood is well lit. Then close it and set the air control.
Blower: wait about 20 minutes after reloading before you turn it back on.
Keep the fire behind the front step. If logs fall against the glass, put them back in place.

Still getting smoke? Make sure kitchen and bathroom exhaust fans are off. They can pull smoke out of the insert.

firstfires.title: Your first few fires
firstfires.html:
A slow start is normal

The refractory bricks that line the firebox hold moisture from manufacturing. It takes a few hot fires to dry them out.

While they're still damp, the bricks look black with smoke deposits. Once the moisture is gone, they turn white.

No break-in needed

Unlike a cast iron stove, this insert doesn't need curing with small fires first. You can light a large fire from the very start.

A slight smell

During the first few fires you'll notice an odor from curing paint and oil burning off the metal. It can be strong enough to set off your smoke detector. Open doors and windows to air out the room.

Before your very first fire, read the manual and make sure the refractory bricks are properly installed inside the firebox.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
This insert burns best with seasoned cordwood.

  • Seasoned means cut, split and dried under cover for at least 6 months, preferably a year or more.
  • Dry seasoned wood is generally under 20% moisture. RSF strongly suggests a wood moisture meter to check.
  • Hardwood is denser than softwood, so a load burns longer and more evenly.

Wet wood is hard to burn and gives little heat. It also builds creosote faster and leaves dark deposits on the glass.

Never burn

Driftwood, treated wood, scrap, coal, garbage or plastic. Large amounts of paper, cardboard, mill ends or construction waste can overfire the insert, or even start a chimney fire if the flue is dirty.

Wax fire logs (like Duraflame) aren't recommended because they dirty the glass. If you use one, burn only one at a time and don't poke or stir it. Use only firelogs evaluated for fireplace use.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
The fire doesn't always run hot enough to keep the glass clean. A good hot fire once a day usually burns off most deposits. The drier the wood and the hotter the fire, the cleaner the glass.

When it needs a clean

  1. Wait until the glass is completely cool. Cleaning hot glass can cause a serious burn.
  2. For light buildup, dampen a ball of newspaper and dip it in the fireplace ashes to make a paste. Scrub the glass with it, then wipe clean.
  3. For heavier buildup, use a wood stove glass cleaner recommended by your dealer.
No abrasive cleaners unless they're made for this use. Don't spray glass cleaner on the painted surfaces; it can strip the paint.

Heat won't break the glass, but impact can. Don't hit it or slam the door. Never use the insert with broken glass. Replacement glass (5mm ceramic) comes only from an authorized RSF dealer.

chimney.title: Ashes & chimney care
chimney.html:
Ashes

  • Take ashes out before they get deep enough to spill when you open the door.
  • Put them in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid, set on a non-combustible floor or the ground, well away from anything that can burn.
  • Keep them in the closed container until all cinders have fully cooled, even if you plan to bury or spread them.

Creosote

Slow fires make tar and vapors that condense in the chimney as creosote. If it catches fire, it burns extremely hot.

  • Check the chimney liner every week or so until you learn how often it needs cleaning.
  • Clean it when the buildup reaches 1/8" (3 mm).

To sweep, the baffle (an insulation panel above the tubes at the top of the firebox) comes out first: remove the front tube, then slide the baffle forward and out through the door. Close the door, remove the chimney cap and sweep with a 6" round soft-bristle brush. Refit the baffle and tube the same way, tube holes facing slightly up, locking pin in.

RSF strongly recommends service by a certified professional.

smoke.title: Smoke or a runaway fire
smoke.html:
Smoke comes in when you open the door

  • Open the door more slowly and let the pressure settle before opening it fully.
  • Turn the blower off (if you have one) before opening the door.
  • Turn off kitchen range hoods and bathroom exhaust fans. Crack a window near the insert until the draft is going, then close it.
  • Use enough kindling to get a hot fire quickly. Smoke is most likely while you're lighting.
  • Make sure the chimney is clean and the cap isn't plugged. Caps with screens clog more easily with creosote.

The fire burns too fast and won't slow down

Air is probably leaking in, most likely at the door. If the air control has no effect at all, stop using the insert until the leak is fixed.

Test the seal: close the door on a sheet of paper, latch it, and pull gently but firmly. You should feel resistance. Repeat all around the door. A worn gasket needs replacing; kits are available from your RSF dealer. A damaged secondary air tube at the top of the firebox can also let in extra air.

safety.title: Safety first
safety.html:
• Keep furniture, firewood and other combustibles at least 4' from the front of the insert.
  • Have at least one smoke detector on each level of your home, and at least one carbon monoxide detector.
  • Burn with the door fully closed. If it's left partly open, gas and flame can be drawn out into the room.
  • Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire. Keep them well away while the insert is in use.
  • Don't use a grate, don't tamper with the air control, and don't add a flue damper.
  • Don't slam the door; it can break the glass. Never run the insert with broken glass.
Don't overfire the insert. Watch for the signs: if you can't slow the fire down, or the chimney connector glows red, the insert is overfiring. Damage from overfiring isn't covered by the warranty.

Burning wood makes carbon monoxide. Keep the door gasket sealing and the chimney joints in good condition.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
RSF warrants its wood-burning appliances against defects in material and workmanship for 30 years. Coverage steps down over time:

First yearDefective parts repaired or replaced, plus reasonable labor
Years 2-5Defective parts repaired or replaced, no labor
Years 6-30Replacement parts, if available, at 50% of retail price, no labor

Not covered

  • Electrical components after one year
  • Glass, plating and andirons
  • Normal wear: paint discoloration, worn gaskets, eroded or cracked refractory
  • Vandalism, neglect, abuse, over-firing, improper fuel or loads, or skipped service
  • Installations that don't follow the manual, damage in transit, and repairs RSF didn't authorize in advance
The warranty isn't transferable. Defective parts are handled through an authorized RSF dealer, and non-genuine parts void the warranty. This is a summary; the full terms are in the manual.

specOutput.title: Heat output
specOutput.html:
Heat delivered11757 to 25406 BTU/h
Average19 077 BTU/h
Maker's website: BTU Maximum 50,000 BTU/h. Based on engineering calculations using firebox volume...

Burn rate is set with the combustion air control: faster fires give more heat but send more hot air up the chimney, so efficiency drops. The optional internal blower (FO-HB1) adds air circulation and marginally more heat output.

specPerf.title: Emissions & efficiency
specPerf.html:
Particulate emissions1.7 grams per hour (2020 EPA standard, crib wood)
Optimal efficiency75.3% (low heating value, best burning conditions)
Weighted average EPA efficiency70% (higher heating value, EPA crib wood)

Both efficiencies use CSA B415.1:22 calculations. Listed by PFS-TECO (PFS mark for Canada and U.S., file F23-112); tested to ULC 628:2022 and UL 1482-2022.

The minimum low burn rate is set by the manufacturer. Federal regulations prohibit altering it; don't tamper with the air control or install a flue damper that would reduce chimney draft.

specLiner.title: Chimney liner
specLiner.html:
A continuous, full-height liner from the insert's flue collar to the top of the masonry chimney, attached at both ends. The insert was tested with a 6" liner for best performance; going below 6" can cause performance issues, and a 5.5" liner needs the taller minimum chimney.

Diameter6" (152 mm) or 5.5" (140 mm)
U.S.Stainless steel, type HT per UL 1777
CanadaClass 3 per CAN/ULC-S635, or CAN/ULC-S640
Flexible linerStove adapter on the bottom before connecting to the flue collar
Never connect to a chimney flue serving another appliance. Seal the damper area around the liner so room air can't pass into the chimney cavity.

specHearth.title: Hearth extension
specHearth.html:
The area immediately in front of the insert must be protected by non-combustible material.

D · Width each side of the masonry hearth opening8" (203 mm)
E · Depth from front of insert door, U.S.16" (406 mm)
E · Depth from front of insert door, Canada18" (457 mm)

Type of protection

Ember protection onlyMin R-value 0 · Type 1 hearth pad sufficient
Floor protection (ember + heat)Min R-value 1.5 · Type 2 hearth pad required
  • Floor-level installation: floor protection, R=1.5.
  • Raised installation, with or without a non-combustible step in front: 5 ¼" or less → floor protection, R=1.5; more than 5 ¼" → ember protection only.

Table 3 keys these cases to lettered dimensions on Figure 4 (p. 8); check the drawing for what is measured. Example R-values (mfg specs): 1/2" Micore 160: 1.27 · 1/2" Micore 300: 1.03 · common brick 2 3/8": 0.475 · 1/2" Durock or HardieBacker cement board: 0.26. U.S.: UL 1618 and NFPA 211; Canada: CAN/CSA-B365.

specMantel.title: Combustible mantel
specMantel.html:
Masonry and other non-combustible mantels (shelf and posts) can go anywhere around the fireplace facing. Combustible shelves follow Table 4; depth is always measured from the face of the masonry fireplace.

Shelf 0" to 8" deep24" above glass top · 42 1/2" above unit bottom
Shelf 9" deep27 7/8" · 46 3/8"
Shelf 10" deep31 3/4" · 50 1/4"
Shelf 11" deep35 3/4" · 54 1/4"
Shelf 12" deep39 1/2" · 58"
Combustible post, 0" to 4" deep9" min from the glass

A shelf with a variable-depth cross-section must keep its widest part no lower than the height for that depth, and its lowest point no lower than the height for its depth at that point.

specOptions.title: Options & parts
specOptions.html:
FO-HB1Internal blower kit · electricity required; plugs into a nearby outlet, no electrician needed
FO-F3600INBPBacking plate (flat) · fills an opening larger than the standard trim
FO-F3600INBP2Deep backing plate (1.5" depth)

Each option ships with its own installation instructions. Use only genuine RSF parts; substitutes void the warranty. The insert hasn't been tested with a gas log set: don't install a gas log set (vented or unvented) or a gas log lighter.

review.notes: Unit dimensions (Figure 1, p. 5), minimum fireplace dimensions (Figure 2, p. 6) and the clearance layout (Figure 3, p. 6) are drawings with no values in the text; not transcribed. The manual text gives no height/width/depth, weight, firebox volume, max log length, view/glass area or heating area, so those catalog fields could not be checked; efficiency 75.3% LHV, 1.7 g/h, 19 077 BTU/h average and the 6" flue match pp. 4 and 11. Table 3 (p. 9) hearth-extension cases key to lettered dimensions on Figure 4 (p. 8); the guide gives the 5 1/4" threshold and says the measured dimension is on the drawing. Table 2 (p. 8): the 0-1000 ft row is split in the text; its straight-chimney value (12') agrees with Table 1 and the +6" per 1000' rule. Only the straight column is quoted; offset columns are referred to the table. U.S. liner spec prints as 'type HT (21000 F)' (p. 11), probably 2100 F with a lost degree sign; the temperature is omitted. Cover (p. 1) reads 'Residential Factory Built Fireplace', while pp. 9-10 say masonry fireplaces only and never into a factory-built fireplace; the guide follows the installation text. 'Pilot' (p. 16) is the metal air tube between the andiron posts, not a gas pilot. Creosote threshold reads 'in excess of 1/8"' (p. 3) and '1/8" or more' (p. 17); treated as the same. Heat figures kept as printed (11757, 25406, '19 077'). No error-code table, so codes is empty. Blower electrical rating not given. Replacement parts (p. 22) and listing label (p. 20) pages carry no parts list or label text beyond the genuine-parts line and the label location. Insert removal (p. 19) and door/glass service are left out of the install sequence. No French or scrambled text.
